hook: A food label says a sweetener is 40% carbon by mass. A forensic lab burns a white powder and weighs the products. In both cases, chemists use mass percents to work out what a substance is made of, atom by atom, and identify it with nothing more than a balance and a periodic table.

prereq.q: How many moles of oxygen atoms are in 8.00 g of oxygen atoms (16.00 g/mol)?
What is the molar mass of CO₂ (C 12.01, O 16.00)?

figure.caption: From mass percents to a formula: grams, then moles, then the smallest whole-number ratio, then the molar mass to scale up.

chain.cause: A pure compound is always made of the same atoms in the same ratio
chain.effect: it always has the same mass percent of each element (law of definite proportions)

chain.cause: Atoms of different elements have different masses
chain.effect: a mass ratio is not an atom ratio, so masses must be converted to moles

chain.cause: Dividing every mole amount by the smallest gives the simplest ratio
chain.effect: that ratio, cleared to whole numbers, is the empirical formula

chain.cause: Many molecules share one empirical formula
chain.effect: the molar mass is needed to find how many empirical units make one molecule

ideas: A pure substance has a fixed composition (law of definite proportions): every sample of water is 11.2% H by mass.
Mass percent of an element = (mass of the element in one formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
Empirical formula: assume 100 g, convert grams to moles, divide by the smallest, clear fractions (×2 for .5, ×3 for .33).
Molecular formula = empirical formula × n, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass.

misconception.wrong: Mass percents give the atom ratio directly, so a compound that is 75% X and 25% Y has three X atoms for each Y.
misconception.right: Different atoms have different masses, so a mass ratio is not an atom ratio. Convert each mass to moles first; only the ratio of moles gives the formula.

summary: A pure compound has a fixed composition by mass. Mass percent is an element's share of the molar mass. To find an empirical formula, convert mass data to moles and reduce to the smallest whole-number ratio. The molar mass then gives the molecular formula, a whole-number multiple of the empirical one.
